body:
Adds `examples/global_wind_driven_gyres.jl`: a four-layer global ocean on a 1° `TripolarGrid` with grid-fitted ETOPO1 bathymetry, a z-star vertical coordinate and a `SplitExplicitFreeSurface`, forced by zonal wind belts and a surface temperature restoring. It runs six years with f = 2Ω sin φ, f = Ω sin φ and f = 2Ω sin 30° (`FPlane`): halving Ω roughly doubles the Gulf Stream and Kuroshio transports, as Sverdrup theory predicts, and without β the gyres are not western-intensified.

- Everything runs in `Float32` on Metal, CUDA or the CPU.
- The wind stress is four Gaussian belts, the trades and westerlies of each hemisphere, following the observed annual- and zonal-mean ocean wind stress from the NCEP/NCAR reanalysis.
- ETOPO1 is read from NCEI over OPeNDAP at three points per cell and averaged in 3 × 3 blocks; `GridFittedBottom` uses `InterfaceImmersedCondition` so that shelf seas and straits stay open. `resolution` is a top-level parameter.
- One animation stacks the surface speed and T − T* (departure from the restoring profile) of the three runs; the barotropic streamfunction is computed with `CumulativeIntegral`.
- The Coriolis force uses `DualGridScheme`, which removes the grid-scale noise of the C-grid Coriolis term at 1°.
- Exports `interpolate!`, which regrids the elevation onto the tripolar grid.

Each run costs about 4 minutes per simulated year on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU (one-hour `SplitRungeKutta3` steps, 79 barotropic substeps), so the three six-year runs take just under two hours.

body:
On a distributed grid stretched in one direction, `ConjugateGradientPoissonSolver` with the FFT preconditioner (`DistributedFourierTridiagonalPoissonSolver`) diverges to a `NaN` residual or stalls, while the same setup on one rank converges in ~10 iterations. Two differences from the serial `FourierTridiagonalPoissonSolver`:

- `compute_preconditioner_rhs!` multiplied the residual by `V⁻¹` only. The tridiagonal system discretizes `Δξᶜ ∇²`, so the right-hand side also needs `Δξᶜ` (as the pressure source term and the serial `set_source_term!` apply); without it the preconditioner is not symmetric on a stretched grid.
- `solve!` returned the solution with an arbitrary constant in the singular Neumann mode (#6163); the serial solver removes the mean, and the distributed one now does too.

Performance: the mean removal is one global reduction and one broadcast per solve, the same `mean` the serial solver already pays. On 2 A100s with a 256×256×2048 stretched immersed grid (ranks bound to 16 cores each), it is 3 ms against a 167 ms preconditioner application and a 103 ms CG iteration, about 3% of the iteration or 50 ms of a 16-iteration, 1.65 s pressure solve. Zeroing the mode in spectral space instead would save the `Allreduce` but needs separate index bookkeeping for each transposed layout.

`test/mpi/conjugate_gradient_solver.jl` gains a z-stretched case; the FFT-preconditioner cases there were all uniform grids.

Checked with 2 ranks: on a 32×32×64 stretched CPU grid the distributed preconditioner now agrees with the serial one to 7e-16 and CG converges in 1 iteration (before: `NaN` at the iteration cap); on 2 GPUs, a 256×256×2048 stretched immersed-boundary Rayleigh–Bénard step takes 33/30 CG iterations, identical to 1 GPU (before: `NaN`). The staircase convection case from `validation/immersed_boundaries`, run with a deterministic grid on 1 and 2 ranks (CPU and GPU, uniform and stretched z), gives fields that agree to ~1e-15 relative with identical per-step CG iteration counts:

![staircase convection, 1 vs 2 GPUs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xkykai/Oceananigans.jl/xk/pr6161-figures/staircase_comparison.png)

Per-grid detail (b, w, p slices and differences, CG iterations, divergence, buoyancy conservation): [isotropic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xkykai/Oceananigans.jl/xk/pr6161-figures/gpu_isotropic.png), [anisotropic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xkykai/Oceananigans.jl/xk/pr6161-figures/gpu_anisotropic.png), [stretched](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xkykai/Oceananigans.jl/xk/pr6161-figures/gpu_stretched.png).

Closes #6163.

body:
This PR allows models with BGC to compute the BGC tendency in a different kernel by returning the tracers to compute the separate tendencies for from `separate_transition_tracers(bgc)`.

This is kind of a hack because I found on ORCA1 with realistic forcing/closures/etc. that BGC with 6 tracers was causing around a 10x slow down relative to physics only, and the tendency kernels were around 10x slower than expected. I think the problem was from register pressure and with this solution I get speedup back to the expected cost (~8% per tracer + a tiny bit from the BGC work).

I don't know if this is just hiding the register pressure problem, or just getting around a true limitation.
title: Optionally compute bgc transitions in a separate kernel

body:
This PR adds no-op methods for scalar and biharmonic diffusivity and viscosity when the scalar is zero. Previously the stencil was computed and then multiplied by zero, for biharmonic this change results in around ~30% time saving per tracer kernel when I tested the diffusivity methods on a H100 with CATKE+GM+biharm+scalar.

Currently to use you have to pass κ=nothing, we could make this the default?

Base computes `cosd(::Float32)` in Float64, and Metal.jl overrides `cos(::Float32)` but not `cosd`, so the discrete-form temperature restoring in `global_wind_driven_gyres.jl` fails to compile on Metal. This puts back `cos(deg2rad(φ))` from b445501e22c420624f8cf82a69b1b7549852f4af, which da97b5d8cca1e73b65403a43e03b524cc495fa9a (a batched review suggestion in #5996) reverted to `cosd`.
